note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: 5-day history of dry cough and “cold” symptoms; presumed viral URTI, no specific trigger/exposure identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Began ≈5 days ago at the start of the weekend; persistent dry “hacking” cough, runny nose, myalgias, intermittent headache, chills. No worsening trend described.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat: mild redness noted by clinician; no soreness reported; no sensation of throat swelling or closure.  
  • Voice: no change.  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia: none.  
  • Drooling: none.  
  • Nasal: rhinorrhea.  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing: none.  
  • Dyspnea: denied.  
  • Swelling: none to lips, tongue, uvula, face.  
  • Ear/neck: no ear pain/hearing change; no neck swelling or palpable lymphadenopathy per patient.  
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: None stated.
- Allergies: Not documented.
- Current medications: 
  • Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  • Lisinopril – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  • Paracetamol (acetaminophen) – dose/route/frequency not documented (taken for current symptoms).  
  • No NSAID use.
- Social context: Consultation conducted remotely; patient alone but in a secure location.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: None reported or seen.
- Airway/breathing: No wheeze or shortness of breath reported; normal work of breathing on video per clinician.
- Pharynx: Clinician observed mild posterior pharyngeal erythema; tonsils not enlarged.
- Neck: Patient unable to feel cervical nodes; none visualized.
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Mental status: Alert, conversant.
- Companion: None present.

Assessment:
- Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold) with dry cough and rhinorrhea; no evidence of bacterial tonsillitis, bronchitis, or lower-airway involvement. Justified by 5-day mild course, absence of dyspnea, wheeze, or purulence, and limited pharyngeal findings.

Plan:
- Symptomatic management: Over-the-counter “Day Nurse/Night Nurse” combination therapy considered safe with current medications; continue paracetamol as needed.
- Red-flag advice: Seek medical review if any of the following occur—shortness of breath, wheeze, new chest pain, symptoms persist >3 weeks, or clinical deterioration.
- No prescription issued at this time.
- Follow-up: Patient to contact primary care service if red flags appear or for reassessment after 3 weeks if symptoms unresolved.

● Missing but expected: allergy history, smoking status, exact medication doses/frequencies, temperature/vitals, vaccination status (e.g., influenza, COVID-19), full ENT examination details (otoscopy, nasal exam).  
● Internal conflicts: None identified.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional minor inaudible segments but key clinical content preserved.
